item.description: Brines generated within deep ice can provide reactive micro-environments for geochemical reactions and dust aggregation, including potentially on Mars and other planetary ice environments, according to micro-scale observations from Antarctic ice cores. The discovery of englacial authigenesis has the potential to reshape our interpretation of insoluble dust records in ice cores and our understanding of planetary ice-bearing deposits on Mars. Mineralogical changes in deep ice involve iron mobilization and transformation driven by the circulation of acidic fluids within the ice matrix, leading to the authigenic formation of jarosite. Here we show that englacial authigenesis is documented across different Antarctic deep ice cores and involves the formation of mineral phases such as goethite/lepidocrocite and hematite/maghemite, in addition to jarosite. The coexistence of these phases reflects micron-scale variability in pH and water activity within the englacial brine network. Englacial authigenesis introduces biases in bulk mineralogical proxies used to reconstruct dust source conditions, and provides a grounded explanation for the anomalously high dust magnetization observed in deep Antarctic ice. We further propose that the repeated burial of dust within planetary ice reservoirs, as expected on Mars over orbital timescales, represents a viable mechanism for the oxidation, aggregation and magnetic activation of Martian airborne dust, without requiring prolonged warm and wet surface conditions. item.title: Cascading magmatic unrest and aseismic faulting in the Aegean Sea enabled by elastic stress relay
item.dc:creator: John D. Wilding
Taiyi A. Wang
Yuan-Kai Liu
Zachary E. Ross
item.description: Magma reservoirs commonly exist in clusters and situate within complex fault networks, yet sequential triggering of unrest at multiple reservoirs and faults is rarely observed. We show that the 2025 earthquake swarm in the Christiana-Santorini-Kolumbo complex of the Aegean Sea was driven by elastic stress transfer between two magma reservoirs, a 9-kilometer-long dike, and a 17-kilometer-long, southeast-dipping fault. Pressurization of the magma reservoir under Santorini triggered a dike intrusion originating from a separate magma reservoir under the Kolumbo volcano. The dike, in turn, triggered a moment magnitude ( M w ) 6.2 aseismic slip transient on a SW-NE trending branch of the Amorgos fault. Episodic bursts of upward-propagating seismicity within the geodetically constrained dike potentially indicate buoyancy-driven, segmented dike opening. We suggest that unrest in rift zones can propagate over spatial scales much larger than individual magma reservoirs and faults via sequential relay of elastic stress. item.title: Magmatic origin of the Dewar magnetic anomaly: Implications for an early lunar dynamo
item.dc:creator: Xi Yang
Anna Mittelholz
Adrien Broquet
Max Moorkamp
item.description: The Moon’s ancient magnetic field provides critical insights into lunar thermal and magnetic evolution, yet the lifetime of the interior dynamo remains debated. Returned samples yield complex and contradictory paleomagnetic records, while orbital data reveal crustal magnetic anomalies of uncertain origin from either a core dynamo or transient impact-generated fields. Here, we jointly invert gravity and magnetic observations in the region around the Dewar swirl, a high-albedo feature associated with the Dewar magnetic anomaly. We identify a shallow, magnetized, high-density body consistent with buried mare basalt. Our estimates require a paleointensity exceeding 11 microtesla, suggesting an active lunar dynamo about 4.2 billion years ago, as constrained by the superposed basin ejecta. The results also show that swirl formation requires horizontal magnetization and iron oxide enrichment. These findings link a magnetic anomaly to its geologic origin and magnetizing field, providing constraints on the lunar magnetic and volcanic history. item.description: Analyses of returned samples from asteroids Bennu and Ryugu reveal notable similarities in chemical and isotopic compositions to Ivuna-type (CI) carbonaceous chondrites, prompting reassessment of their origin. We present nucleosynthetic iron (Fe), titanium (Ti), and chromium (Cr) isotope data for Bennu. Minor Cr isotope variations among aliquots likely reflect parent body aqueous alteration, whereas Fe and Ti isotope data are homogeneous and indistinguishable from those of Ryugu and CI chondrites at bulk (>20 milligrams) scale. These results demonstrate that CI-like bodies accreted from a common dust reservoir with affinities to both inner (noncarbonaceous) and outer (carbonaceous) Solar System materials. Combined isotopic, petrographic, and chemical evidence suggests formation near the water ice line inside proto-Jupiter’s orbit, where Jupiter’s growth restricted the inward drift of larger particles, whereas efficient mixing of fine-grained dust produced bodies with near-solar compositions. item.title: Pacific tsunami records suggest similar rupture locations of two great Kamchatka earthquakes only 73 years apart
item.dc:creator: Matías Carvajal
Kelin Wang
Alejandra Gubler

item.description: Whether seismic slip can far exceed the slip budget of a subduction megathrust over a short time has important implications to earthquake physics and hazards. The first modern test comes from two great Kamchatka earthquakes of moment magnitude 8.8 to 9.0 in 1952 and 2025. Here, we use tide gauge tsunami records across the Pacific to determine whether the two events ruptured the same or complementary fault areas. We extract records of the 1952 tsunami from analog marigrams at 52 tide gauge stations and minimize their time uncertainties by matching hindcast tides. The 1952 tsunami waveforms and travel times are remarkably similar to those of the 2025 event. Tsunami modeling shows that a range of relative rupture locations can produce the waveform similarity, but only nearly colocated ruptures can explain the travel time similarity. On the basis of conventional rationale, the 2025 earthquake consumed more than twice the megathrust slip deficit accrued since 1952. We explain the conundrum by fast energy accumulation in a viscoelastic Earth. Published: 2026-09-23T17:59:49+00:00 Venue: Science Advances Score: 0.539 (flagship)

item.title: Staking out the frontiers: The limits of the metazoan shallow marine fossil record
item.dc:creator: Thomas A. Neubauer
Mathias Harzhauser
item.description: The fossil record is inherently incomplete, yet its physical limits remain largely uncharted. Here, we quantify the spatiotemporal coverage of the global shallow-marine metazoan fossil record across the Phanerozoic, using a large dataset of georeferenced collections intersected with global geological data. Modeling historical sampling trajectories, we show that for most time intervals, future data accumulation is expected to be negligible, and geographic coverage is approaching saturation. For intervals with remaining potential, we reconstruct the present-day extent of unexplored but geologically accessible strata, providing spatially explicit guidance on where undetected fossil information is most likely to await discovery. Our results constitute a quantitative roadmap for prioritizing fieldwork, completing occurrence databases, and mobilizing unpublished museum collections. item.title: Gravitational torque drives multidecadal variations in length of day
item.dc:creator: Huifeng Zhang
Mathieu Dumberry
item.description: Fluctuations in the length of day (LOD) on decadal timescales are caused primarily by an exchange of angular momentum between the Earth’s mantle and core^ 1 – 3 . Several mechanisms have been proposed to explain this exchange, including electromagnetic^ 4 – 7 and topographic^ 8 – 10 coupling at the core–mantle boundary (CMB) and a gravitational torque by the inner core^ 11 , 12 . However, the precise nature of the core–mantle torque remains unknown. Here we show that the seismically reconstructed differential rotation of the inner core^ 13 – 15 and core flows derived from magnetic field changes^ 16 , 17 suggest that the multidecadal LOD changes are driven primarily by the gravitational torque and resisted by electromagnetic and topographic torques, consistent with results from Earth-like dynamo models^ 18 . Our reconstructed torque histories, although tied to the accuracy of the inner core rotation and core flow models, support a lowermost mantle that features near-neutrally buoyant thermochemical piles^ 19 – 21 , a post-perovskite (pPv) phase with a low viscosity^ 22 and a highly conducting^ 23 , 24 iron-enriched layer a few kilometres thick at its base^ 25 . Our results also suggest a low-viscosity inner core deforming in only a few years^ 26 – 28 and yield an upper limit on the stratification at the top of the fluid core. Altogether, our study contributes to bringing into focus an emerging picture of the deepest regions of our planet. Multidecadal fluctuations in Earth’s length of day are shown to be driven by gravitational torque and resisted by electromagnetic and topographic forces, improving our understanding of the material properties and dynamics of Earth’s deep interior. item.dc:creator: Li-Juan Xu

item.description: 3.48 billion year old volcanic rocks reveal that Earth’s deep mantle became progressively more oxidized over time, a shift closely linked to the rise of oxygen in Earth’s early atmosphere. The evolution of Earth’s mantle redox state is central to understanding the rise of atmospheric oxygen and the development of a habitable planet. However, whether the deep mantle has become increasingly oxidized over geological time and its underlying mechanisms remain debated. Here, we analyze chromium isotopes in 66 ancient volcanic rocks (komatiites and picrites) spanning from 3.48 to 1.87 billion years ago combined with an oxygen fugacity (fO_2) estimate (Fe^3+/ΣFe) derived from thermodynamic simulations. We find that older Archean samples possess distinct isotopic signatures compared to younger Paleoproterozoic ones. Our modeling indicates that Archean magmas formed under more reducing conditions, driven by less recycled surface material in the deep Earth. These results provide evidence for an oxidation of the mantle from Archean to Paleoproterozoic. Our results link deep geodynamic transitions to the surface Great Oxidation Event through the progressive evolution of the mantle redox state. item.title: Coupled increases in pelagic fish productivity and export productivity during the Paleocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum
item.dc:creator: Xiuwen Zhou
Ruiling Zhang
Man-Yin Tsang
Mingsong Li
Weiqi Yao
item.description: Ocean productivity is sensitive to climate change, and its decline in recent decades has profoundly impacted the biosphere. Yet its long-term trajectory under global warming remains a topic lacking consensus. To address this question, we use paired ichthyolith and marine barite accumulation rates to investigate marine productivity and associated biological responses during the Paleocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum. We find a widespread increase in pelagic fish productivity, particularly in the Pacific and North Atlantic, that closely tracks export productivity in trend and spatial pattern, suggesting this increase was fueled by enhanced carbon export from the surface ocean. Model simulations support the observed trend, demonstrating that under elevated p CO_2 conditions, the effects of enhanced nutrient supply can outweigh the suppressive effects of ocean stratification on export productivity. Our findings highlight that the long-term response of marine productivity to sustained greenhouse warming may differ fundamentally from the short-term declines observed in the modern ocean. Increased productivity and fish abundance in the open ocean during extreme warming 56 million years ago contrasted with the short-term declines observed today, highlighting that marine ecosystems may respond differently to prolonged global warming. item.title: Divergent deep-sea temperatures in the Pacific and Atlantic during the onset of Antarctic glaciation
item.dc:creator: Victoria E. Taylor
Alison M. Piasecki
Eivind O. Straume

item.description: Approximately 34 million years ago at the Eocene–Oligocene transition, Earth cooled sufficiently to sustain a large-scale Antarctic ice sheet. Our understanding of this climatic pivot point relies heavily on oxygen isotope records from deep-sea dwelling benthic foraminifera (δ^18O_b), which document a globally synchronous increase, interpreted to reflect a combination of deep-sea cooling and ice-sheet growth. Here we present benthic foraminiferal clumped isotope-derived deep-sea temperature records from two ocean basins, spanning the Eocene–Oligocene transition. Our records from the equatorial Pacific and North Atlantic exhibit divergent temperature behaviour, in contrast to similar δ^18O_b signals, with earlier Pacific and later Atlantic cooling compared with the δ^18O_b increase. These differences are probably masked in the δ^18O_b records by contrasting salinity gradients required to maintain similar densities. A reversed interbasin temperature gradient relative to today, with an overall cooler deep North Atlantic, suggests a very different deep-ocean structure, with potentially two different southern-sourced deep-water masses. The divergent properties of these two water masses may reflect different interactions between the temporally and spatially variable early cryosphere and deep-water formation regions, indicating a direct influence of the cryosphere on deep-water properties. Deep-sea temperatures in the Pacific Ocean and North Atlantic Ocean responded differently to the expansion of the Antarctic ice sheet at the Eocene–Oligocene transition, according to benthic foraminiferal clumped isotope records. item.title: Cosmogenic radiocarbon production and glacial cycles control marine radiocarbon archive variations
item.dc:creator: M. Butzin
F. Adolphi
G. Lohmann
item.description: Abstract Marine radiocarbon archives are depleted relative to the atmosphere, which is commonly expressed as the marine radiocarbon reservoir age. Here we apply an Earth system model of intermediate complexity equipped with radiocarbon to simulate marine reservoir ages over the past 50,000 years. Globally, our simulated reservoir ages range from 400 to 1200 years at the sea surface and are systematically lower than previous uncoupled model estimates. This is mainly due to stronger vertical mixing and air sea exchange rates of carbon dioxide in our model. Short-term reservoir age variations are dominated by changes in cosmogenic radiocarbon production, while glacial-interglacial climate variations exert slower and damped effects. item.description: Most coastal areas of the United States are sinking, with the Gulf Coast and disadvantaged communities facing the highest risk, according to an analysis of more than 190 million satellite and ground-based measurements of land elevation change. item.description: Accretion and early evolution of rocky planets involved high temperatures that produced global magma oceans. item.description: Abstract Geophysical observations from the InSight mission suggest anomalously low seismic velocities near the Martian core–mantle boundary, possibly indicating a molten silicate layer. item.description: Slab-derived supercritical fluids serve as important agents for material transport in deep subduction zones. item.description: Titanium-rich phases in subducting oceanic crust are key hosts for high field strength elements (HFSEs) and molybdenum, and potential carriers of water to the deep mantle. item.description: Metamorphic fluid-rock interactions make key contributions to the global carbon cycle and can transport and deposit critical elements, so it is necessary to examine these interactions quantitatively. item.description: The Banded Gneissic Complex-I (BGC I) of the Aravalli Craton (NW India) preserves a Neoarchean (>2.6 Ga) volcano-sedimentary association whose mafic component (metabasites) offers a rare window into early-Earth geodynamics. item.description: Archean cratons are at the core, in terms of both their geographical position and geological processes, of the first long-lived lithospheric units. Our results indicate that the Hf-isotope signature of igneous zircon domains from these high grade meta-sedimentary rocks is similar to the Hf-isotope signatures of coeval igneous zircon located further south and unambiguously distinct from that of the Central zone of the Limpopo belt. item.description: Mineral carbonation, which transforms CO_2 into stable carbonates via reaction with Ca- and Mg-silicates, offers a permanent and secure carbon sequestration pathway. Olivine is a highly reactive feedstock, and its carbonation kinetics are known to depend on particle size, CO_2 partial pressure ( $${P_{{\rm CO}_2}}$$ P CO 2 ), temperature, and additives. However, two key gaps persist in the current understanding. First, the time-dependent influence of $${P_{{\rm CO}_2}}$$ P CO 2 throughout the carbonation process remains unclear. Furthermore, the effect of the grinding method (wet vs. dry) is frequently oversimplified as reducing particle size, neglecting its concurrent alteration of other physicochemical properties. This study systematically addresses these gaps by investigating the carbonation of fine-grained olivine under varied $${P_{{\rm CO}_2}}$$ P CO 2 (5–14 MPa) at 185 °C. Reaction progress was tracked in real time using a flush-sampling batch reactor. Our results reveal that the wet-ground olivine, possessing a higher specific surface area (SSA), achieved significantly greater carbonation efficiency compared to the dry-ground sample. Kinetic analysis based on the shrinking core model (SCM) indicates that the formed porous carbonate layer does not act as a diffusion barrier but facilitates the reaction. Increasing $${P_{{\rm CO}_2}}$$ P CO 2 significantly enhanced the carbonation rate and final efficiency, with the maximum conversion reaching 98.45% at 14 MPa after 8 h. Furthermore, we identified that the reaction was most sensitive to $${P_{{\rm CO}_2}}$$ P CO 2 during the initial stage, with the most pronounced effect observed within the first hour. The primary mechanistic insight is that initial carbonation is predominantly controlled by $${P_{{\rm CO}_2}}$$ P CO 2 -driven dissolution, whereas at later stages, the available reactive surface area becomes the limiting factor. This work demonstrates that optimizing both the grinding method (preferring wet grinding for ex-situ applications) and employing elevated $${P_{{\rm CO}_2}}$$ P CO 2 (⩾ 8 MPa for in-situ scenarios) are critical strategies for enhancing the efficiency and practical viability of olivine-based CO_2 sequestration. item.description: The production and differentiation of felsic magmas are one of the key features of continental crust on Earth. Understanding the processes and mechanisms of highly differentiated magmas is crucial for unraveling lithospheric architecture and deep Earth processes, deciphering the evolution of transcrustal magmatic systems, and exploring the metallogenesis of critical metals. Granitic rocks widely occur in China, where their precursor magmas exhibit particularly pronounced differentiation. The highly differentiated granites are common in South China, the Himalaya, Xinjiang (Central Asia), and the Great Xing’an Range. They exhibit diverse characteristics, complex geological settings and significant mineralization potential, thus requiring further investigation. In this paper we present a review of recent progress in experimental petrology related to the formation of highly differentiated granites and outline their diagnostic mineralogical and geochemical indicators. We systematically analyze the spatiotemporal distribution, geochemical signatures, and formation mechanisms of highly differentiated granites in the above four regions. We suggest that such petrogenetic and metallogenic diversities are governed by multiple factors, including source compositions, tectonic setting, and heat and volatile supply. We identify some main challenges for the further study of highly differentiated intracontinental magmas: (1) experiments and simulations on key processes of crust-derived magmas; (2) clarifying spatiotemporal distribution patterns of highly differentiated granites; (3) understanding the physical mechanisms of crystal–melt separation; (4) constraining source nature and melting processes; and (5) constructing transcrustal magmatic system models. Addressing these issues may provide valuable insights into continental crust evolution and associated metallogenic diversity. item.description: Large Igneous Provinces (LIPs) are associated with dramatic changes to the Earth system; their rapid release of carbon may initiate catastrophic climatic changes causing mass extinction. This carbon release is often associated with volcanic emissions, yet metamorphic carbon production is poorly constrained. Metamorphic carbon devolatilization occurs as intrusions interact with host sediment, potentially releasing substantial sedimentary carbon. While this process has been modeled, few studies use an observational approach. Here, we apply geochemical analysis, petrographic analysis, Raman spectroscopy, vitrinite reflectance, and thermodynamic modeling to understand carbon devolatilization in sediment adjacent to Central Atlantic Magmatic Province basaltic intrusions using two boreholes that penetrate the Florida basement. Ultimately, we estimate 220 mols/m2 to 9900 mols/m2 of carbon were mobilized from sedimentary carbonate. Uncertainties in the extent of re‑carbonation suggest that anywhere from 0 mols/m2 to 7100 mols/m2 may have escaped to the surface. We find little evidence of organic carbon mobility, due partly to the increased activity of CO2 from carbonate devolatilization. Discrepancies between measured temperatures and 1D thermal models suggest complexities in heat transport through aqueous pore fluid flow and short (hundred to thousand year) heating timescales. These results highlight that further field-based study can help clarify the roles that heating timescales, fluid flow, sediment chemistry, and other factors play in releasing and capturing carbon during LIP emplacement. item.description: Calc-silicate rocks constitute a significant proportion of the metamorphic basement in the eastern Alxa Block and are key to deciphering its P–T evolution and tectonic history. Isotopically, they exhibit near-chondritic to mildly radiogenic εNd (−0.3 to 2.6), indicating only moderate isotopic enrichment relative to the contemporaneous depleted mantle. However, the major and trace element data indicate derivation from a fertile, enriched mantle source (likely from a garnet pyroxenite source lithology) in the sub-lithospheric mantle. The occurrence of OIB-like magmatism within thick cratonic lithosphere likely highlights the presence of a localized lithospheric thinning. We propose that plume-derived melts exploited such lithospheric ‘thinspots,’ enabling their ascent with minimal lithospheric interaction, in contrast to the coeval tholeiitic magmas. Coeval (ca.1.8 Ga) Paleoproterozoic alkaline mafic–ultramafic magmatism (lamprophyres and orangeites) in the Yilgarn Craton (Australia) additionally reinforces the tectonomagmatic link between the southern Indian Shield and the Yilgarn Craton during the assembly of the Nuna/Columbia supercontinent.
